{"id":"q43","type":"failure","claims":["c5","c6","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"The drift curve compares different groups of dialogues at each d. Given the paper's secret-type finding, how could this curve show a spurious drift effect, or hide a real one?","answer":"Secret type is sampled per dialogue, so the drift groups (142 to 197 dialogues each) can differ in their mix of SSNs, cards, emails and phones. Secret type strongly determines leakage. A drift group that happens to contain more emails or phones would show higher leakage regardless of d, which could create fluctuations or mask a real decay.","rubric":["Identifies imbalance in the secret-type mix across drift groups as the source of a spurious or masked effect","Links this to the strong dependence of leakage on secret type (semi-public types leak more)","Notes that drift groups consist of different dialogues, so composition is not held fixed across d"]},
{"id":"q44","type":"failure","claims":["c7","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"For one persuasion level, suppose a model has L(0)=0.05. Why would Privacy Half-Life almost certainly fail to credit this model even if it nearly stops leaking after drift?","answer":"The threshold is δ=0.1×0.05=0.005. Each drift group has about 142 to 181 responses per persuasion level, so a single leak gives a rate of about 0.0055 to 0.007, which is above δ. τ would therefore require zero leaks at that d and at every larger d, and a single stray leak censors τ at 7.","rubric":["Concludes that τ would likely be censored or fail to credit near-complete suppression","Computes δ=0.005 and notes that one leak in roughly 142 to 181 responses already exceeds it","Notes that the condition requires essentially zero leaks at the qualifying d and at all larger observed d"]},
{"id":"q45","type":"failure","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"An outside group re-queries the same three models through OpenRouter a year later on the identical 1,000 dialogues. Why might they fail to reproduce the reported dialogue-level leakage rates, even with no change to the pipeline?","answer":"The models are API-served and may change over time, so new queries can produce different responses. The reproducible artifact is the logged cached responses with model identifiers and timestamps, not a fresh run.","rubric":["Says the rates may not be reproduced on re-query","Gives the reason: API-served models can be updated or changed over time","Notes that reproducibility rests on the cached responses and logged identifiers rather than on new queries"]},
{"id":"q46","type":"failure","claims":["c5","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Suppose the chi-square test between drift length and leakage had come out significant for a model. Why would that alone fail to show that leakage decays as drift grows?","answer":"A chi-square test of independence is non-directional across the six levels. A significant result could come from d=0, which has no drift turns and only about 44 words, differing from all other levels, or from a non-monotone pattern. It does not establish a graded decrease with d.","rubric":["Concludes that significance does not establish decay or a monotone decrease","Explains that the chi-square test is non-directional or omnibus across the six levels","Notes that the effect could come from d=0 differing structurally (no drift, very short) or from a non-monotone pattern"]},
{"id":"q47","type":"failure","claims":["c2","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"What kind of judge behavior would make the hybrid rates overstate leakage, and which reported check would most directly reveal it?","answer":"A lenient Llama judge that labels regex-negative responses as leaks when they do not reveal the secret would inflate the hybrid rates, because judge positives can only add leaks. The judge-independent fuzzy-matching rates at 0.85 and 0.80 would then fall well below the hybrid rates, exposing the gap.","rubric":["Identifies judge false positives on regex-negative responses (a lenient judge) as the cause of overstatement","Explains that the judge can only raise labels, so its errors add spurious leaks","Names the fuzzy-matching check (0.85/0.80) as the check that would expose it, through fuzzy rates well below hybrid"]},
{"id":"q48","type":"why","claims":["c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Why do the approximate token counts in Tables 1 and 7 take values such as 57.33 for the shortest dialogue and exactly 1060.00 for the longest?","answer":"The token counts are estimated from word counts using a fixed ratio of 4/3 tokens per word. 43 words × 4/3 = 57.33 and 795 words × 4/3 = 1060, so they are not measured tokenizer counts.","rubric":["States that tokens were derived from words by a fixed multiplier of about 4/3 (1.33 tokens per word)","Shows the arithmetic link, e.g. 795×4/3=1060 or 43×4/3=57.33, and notes these are estimates rather than real tokenizer counts"]},
{"id":"q49","type":"why","claims":["c4","c5","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Why are the persuasion-level comparisons better controlled than the drift-length comparisons in PrivDrift?","answer":"Persuasion is varied within each dialogue: all three probes are applied to the same history and secret, which gives matched triples. Drift length is a property of each dialogue, so different d values are compared across different dialogues with different secrets, topics and personas.","rubric":["Concludes that persuasion comparisons are within-dialogue (paired) while drift comparisons are between-dialogue","Explains that the paired design holds the secret and history fixed for persuasion, whereas drift groups differ in secret, topic and persona"]},
{"id":"q50","type":"why","claims":["c2"],"pair":null,"question":"In the McNemar comparison of regex and hybrid labels, why can the discordant pairs occur in only one direction?","answer":"The judge is applied only to regex-negative responses, so it can turn a negative into a positive but can never overturn a regex positive. The only possible discordance is regex-negative with hybrid-positive.","rubric":["States that all discordant cases are regex-negative/hybrid-positive (never the reverse)","Explains that the judge sees only regex-negative responses and so can only add leaks"]},
{"id":"q51","type":"why","claims":["c3","c4"],"pair":null,"question":"Why can a model's dialogue-level any-probe leakage rate never exceed the sum of its simple, medium and hard probe-level leakage rates?","answer":"A dialogue counts as leaking only if at least one of its three probes leaks, so every leaking dialogue contributes at least one leak to the probe-level counts. The share of dialogues with any leak is therefore at most the sum of the three per-probe shares. The rates are equal only when no dialogue leaks on more than one probe.","rubric":["States that the any-probe rate is bounded above by the sum of the three probe-level rates","Explains that each leaking dialogue contributes at least one probe-level leak, so the union cannot exceed the sum (overlap makes it smaller)"]},
{"id":"q52","type":"why","claims":["c1","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Why can the per-drift dialogue lengths in Table 7 be read as the distance between the secret and the probe?","answer":"The secret is inserted in the opening turn and the probe is appended at the end of the transcript. Essentially the whole dialogue therefore lies between disclosure and probe, so dialogue length approximates that distance.","rubric":["Concludes that dialogue length approximates secret-to-probe distance","Explains this by the secret being in the opening turn and the probe being appended at the end"]},
{"id":"q53","type":"why","claims":["c7","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Why is the d=0 condition indispensable for computing Privacy Half-Life, even though the metric is about drift?","answer":"The safety threshold is defined relative to immediate recall as δ=0.1×L(0). Without d=0 there would be no baseline leakage rate from which to set the threshold.","rubric":["States that τ cannot be computed (no threshold) without d=0","Explains that δ is defined as 0.1×L(0), the leakage at d=0"]},
{"id":"q54","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c7"],"pair":"p1","question":"A model has L(0)=0.60 and L(2), L(3), L(4), L(5), L(6) all equal to 0.05. Would its Privacy Half-Life be 2?","answer":"Yes. δ=0.1×0.60=0.06, and every observed d≥2 has leakage 0.05≤0.06, so the smallest qualifying d is 2.","rubric":["Answers yes, τ=2","Computes δ=0.06 and notes that all values from d=2 onward are at or below it"]},
{"id":"q55","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c7"],"pair":"p1","question":"A model has L(0)=0.40 and L(2), L(3), L(4), L(5), L(6) all equal to 0.05. Would its Privacy Half-Life be 2?","answer":"No. δ=0.1×0.40=0.04, and every drift level has leakage 0.05>0.04, so no d qualifies and τ is censored at 7.","rubric":["Answers no; τ is 7 (censored)","Computes δ=0.04 and notes that 0.05 exceeds it at every observed d"]},
{"id":"q56","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2"],"pair":"p2","question":"Could an error by the Llama judge lower the hybrid label of a response that contains the normalized secret?","answer":"No. A response containing the normalized secret is regex-positive and is never sent to the judge, so its hybrid label is fixed as leakage.","rubric":["Answers no","Explains that regex-positive responses bypass the judge, so judge errors cannot affect them"]},
{"id":"q57","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2"],"pair":"p2","question":"Could an error by the Llama judge raise the hybrid label of a response that does not reveal the secret?","answer":"Yes. Such a response is regex-negative and goes to the judge, and a judge false positive would mark it as leakage under the hybrid label.","rubric":["Answers yes","Explains that regex-negative responses are judged, so a judge false positive adds a spurious leak"]},
{"id":"q58","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2"],"pair":"p3","question":"The phone secret is stored as '555-123-4567' and the model replies '+1 (555) 123-4567'. Would Stage 1 flag leakage?","answer":"Yes. Stripping non-digits gives 5551234567 for the secret and 15551234567 for the response, and the secret's digits are a substring of the response's digits.","rubric":["Answers yes","Explains that after digit stripping, the secret's digit string is contained in the response's longer digit string"]},
{"id":"q59","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c2"],"pair":"p3","question":"The phone secret is stored as '+1 555 123 4567' and the model replies '(555) 123-4567'. Would Stage 1 flag leakage?","answer":"No. The normalized secret is 15551234567 and the normalized response is 5551234567. The longer secret string is not a substring of the shorter response, so only the judge could catch it.","rubric":["Answers no (Stage 1 does not flag it)","Explains that the normalized secret includes the extra leading 1, so it is not a substring of the response's digits"]},
{"id":"q60","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c7"],"pair":"p4","question":"A model currently has τ=4. A new drift level d=8 is added, and the model's L(8) is at or below δ. Would its τ remain 4?","answer":"Yes. d=4 still satisfies L(d)≤δ, and every larger observed d (5, 6 and the new 8) is also at or below δ, so the minimum qualifying d is unchanged.","rubric":["Answers yes, τ stays 4","Explains that the stability condition still holds for all larger observed d including 8"]},
{"id":"q61","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c7"],"pair":"p4","question":"A model currently has τ=4. A new drift level d=8 is added, and the model's L(8) is above δ. Would its τ remain 4?","answer":"No. Every candidate d below 8 now has a larger observed drift (d=8) above δ, and d=8 itself fails. The qualifying set is empty, so τ becomes max(D_obs)+1=9.","rubric":["Answers no; τ becomes 9","Explains that the resurgence at d=8 disqualifies all smaller d, and the censored value is max(D_obs)+1"]},
{"id":"q62","type":"transfer","claims":["c1","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"An assistant keeps only the most recent 512 tokens of conversation. Using Table 7, at which drift levels would the typical PrivDrift dialogue lose the secret before the probe, and what does that mean for applying PrivDrift's drift results to this assistant?","answer":"At d=4, 5 and 6 the average lengths (about 603, 695 and 757 tokens) exceed 512. Because the secret sits in the opening turn, it would usually be cut. d=0, 2 and 3 average below 512, though some d=3 dialogues may exceed it. The full-transcript assumption breaks, so PrivDrift's results do not describe this assistant at higher d.","rubric":["Identifies d=4, 5 and 6 (averages above 512 tokens) as typically losing the secret, with d=3 and below mostly retaining it","Reasons from the opening-turn position of the secret and the Table 7 token averages","Concludes that the full-transcript results do not transfer for those drift levels"]},
{"id":"q63","type":"transfer","claims":["c2","c8","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"A team extends PrivDrift to unstructured secrets such as a disclosed health condition. Which detector layer would carry most of the leakage detection, and what consequence follows for label reliability?","answer":"The LLM judge (Stage 2) would carry most of the detection. Stage 1 normalization-substring matching, and to a lesser extent fuzzy matching, depend on fixed-format strings and would rarely fire on paraphrased health information. The labels would then depend heavily on the judge's own error profile, and the paper reports no human agreement for that judge.","rubric":["Names the LLM judge (Stage 2) as carrying most detection","Explains that regex and fuzzy matching rely on fixed-format string overlap and miss paraphrased unstructured content","Notes that labels would then hinge on judge error, which is not validated against humans"]},
{"id":"q64","type":"transfer","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"One company's assistant mostly receives customers' email addresses and phone numbers. Another's mostly receives SSNs and card numbers. Based on PrivDrift, which deployment should expect more re-disclosure after topic drift, and why?","answer":"The email/phone deployment should expect more re-disclosure. PrivDrift finds that secret type strongly determines leakage and that models treat emails and phones as semi-public, while SSNs and cards are protected as canonical identifiers.","rubric":["Chooses the email/phone deployment as the higher-risk one","Cites the secret-type finding that emails and phones are treated as semi-public while SSNs and cards are more protected"]},
{"id":"q65","type":"transfer","claims":["c1","c7"],"pair":null,"question":"A team builds a 500-dialogue version of PrivDrift with the same drift sampling distribution. Roughly how many dialogues should they expect at d=0 and at each nonzero d, and how does this affect Privacy Half-Life?","answer":"They should expect about 100 dialogues at d=0 (0.2×500) and about 80 at each of d=2 to 6 (0.8×500/5). L(0), which sets δ, and each L(d) would be estimated from fewer responses. The threshold and the stability check become noisier, and a single leak moves a rate by about 1.25 percentage points.","rubric":["Gives about 100 at d=0 and about 80 per nonzero d","Explains that δ depends on L(0) and that the stability check depends on each L(d), so smaller groups make τ noisier or coarser"]},
{"id":"q66","type":"transfer","claims":["c2","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"A team runs PrivDrift on four models and wants all pairwise comparisons of leakage on the same dialogues, following the paper's statistical protocol. Which test should they use, and at what per-comparison significance level for an overall 0.05?","answer":"They should use McNemar's test on matched examples, since all models see identical dialogues, with Bonferroni correction. Four models give 6 pairwise comparisons, so each test uses α≈0.05/6≈0.0083.","rubric":["Names McNemar's test on paired or matched responses","Applies Bonferroni over 6 comparisons, giving about 0.0083 per test"]},
{"id":"q67","type":"transfer","claims":["c3","c4"],"pair":null,"question":"A defender wants to decide which interaction style (direct, justified or pressured) to harden their model against first. Should they rely on PrivDrift's dialogue-level leakage rate, and why?","answer":"No. They should use the probe-level per-persuasion rates. The dialogue-level rate counts a dialogue if any of the three probes leaks, so it merges the styles and cannot show which style elicits the secret.","rubric":["Concludes that the probe-level persuasion breakdown should be used instead of the dialogue-level rate","Explains that the dialogue-level any-probe rate pools all three probe styles"]},
{"id":"q68","type":"connect","claims":["c5","c7"],"pair":null,"question":"Suppose leakage had risen steadily with drift length for every model. Would this undermine the drift-length finding or the censored Privacy Half-Life finding?","answer":"Neither would be undermined. Rising leakage is still consistent with drift not reliably reducing leakage. It also means leakage never settles below 0.1×L(0), so τ would still be censored at 7.","rubric":["Concludes that neither finding is undermined","Explains that an increase is compatible with 'no reliable decrease' and leaves τ censored because stable suppression is never reached"]},
{"id":"q69","type":"connect","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"If one model's 95% bootstrap confidence interval for dialogue-level hybrid leakage had included zero, which of the paper's conclusions would lose support, and for which model?","answer":"The claim that all three models leak substantially at the dialogue level would lose support for that model, since its leakage would not be distinguishable from zero.","rubric":["Names the claim that all models leak substantially at the dialogue level","Explains that a CI including zero means leakage is not distinguishable from zero for that model"]},
{"id":"q70","type":"connect","claims":["c2","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Suppose the leaks added by the Llama judge (hybrid minus regex) turned out to be almost entirely email responses. Which conclusion would then rest partly on the judge rather than on deterministic matching?","answer":"The secret-type finding that emails leak more than SSNs and cards would rest partly on the judge. The per-type breakdown uses hybrid labels, so much of the email-versus-numeric gap would come from judge positives rather than from regex-confirmed disclosures.","rubric":["Names the secret-type contrast (emails treated as semi-public, leaking more)","Explains that the per-type rates use hybrid labels, so the gap would depend on judge-added leaks"]},
{"id":"q71","type":"connect","claims":["c2"],"pair":null,"question":"If a reported table showed a model's regex leakage rate exceeding its hybrid rate, which property of the detector would be violated, and which interpretation from Section 5.1 would become invalid?","answer":"The property that the hybrid label is never below the regex label would be violated, because the judge only adds positives to regex-negatives. This would signal a pipeline or bookkeeping error. The reading of the hybrid-minus-regex difference as the judge's contribution would no longer be valid.","rubric":["Identifies the violated property that hybrid can never be lower than regex","Concludes that the difference could no longer be read as the judge's contribution (or that it indicates a computation error)"]},
{"id":"q72","type":"connect","claims":["c3","c4"],"pair":null,"question":"If every model's dialogue-level leakage rate had exactly equalled its simple-probe leakage rate, what would that imply about the contribution of the medium and hard probes to dialogue-level vulnerability?","answer":"It would imply that the medium and hard probes add no newly vulnerable dialogues. Any dialogue they cracked was already cracked by the direct query, so dialogue-level vulnerability would be fully explained by the simple probe.","rubric":["Concludes that the justified and pressured probes add no extra leaking dialogues beyond the simple probe","Explains that dialogue-level leakage is the union of probes, so equality with the simple rate means the other probes only leak where the simple probe already did"]},
{"id":"q73","type":"connect","claims":["c4"],"pair":null,"question":"If the post-hoc McNemar tests had found the same significant pairs, in the same direction, for all three models, which part of the persuasion claim would be undermined?","answer":"The claim that persuasion affects leakage differently by model would be undermined, since all three models would show an identical pattern. Non-monotonicity could still hold if the shared pattern was not ordered.","rubric":["Names the 'differently by model' part of the persuasion claim","Explains that an identical pairwise pattern across models contradicts model-specific effects"]},
{"id":"q74","type":"scope","claims":["c1","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that each additional drift turn adds a roughly constant amount of context between the secret and the probe? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Contradicted. Table 7 shows uneven increments in average words: about 90 from d=2 to 3, 108 from 3 to 4, 69 from 4 to 5 and only 47 from 5 to 6. Added distance per turn is not constant.","rubric":["Answers contradicted","Cites the uneven Table 7 increments, e.g. shrinking growth from d=5 to d=6 (about 47 words) versus about 108 from d=3 to d=4"]},
{"id":"q75","type":"scope","claims":["c3","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that the measured leakage rates count inappropriate information flows in the contextual-integrity sense? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. A leak is any re-disclosure of the secret in response to a probe. The paper explicitly does not adjudicate whether reuse matches the purpose of the original disclosure (e.g. a justified form request), so some counted leaks might be norm-consistent.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Explains that leakage labels count any re-disclosure, while the paper explicitly does not judge contextual norms or purpose consistency"]},
{"id":"q76","type":"scope","claims":["c3","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper establish which of the three models leaks the most? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The result tables report only the reporting structure (e.g. 'Any-probe rate', 'Per-type rate') without numeric values, so no ranking of models can be drawn from the paper.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Explains that no numeric per-model rates are reported in the tables"]},
{"id":"q77","type":"scope","claims":["c1","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show how models re-disclose secrets when the request comes from a tool output or retrieved document rather than from a user turn? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. Such scenarios motivate the work, but the evaluation appends standardized probes to the transcript at three persuasion levels and does not test tool-mediated or injected instructions.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Explains that only standardized appended probes were evaluated, not tool-output or prompt-injection channels"]},
{"id":"q78","type":"scope","claims":["c1","c4","c5","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that the dialogue topic (e.g. tax filing versus medical triage) affects leakage? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. Topic is used to condition the drift turns, but the analyses group leakage only by drift length, persuasion level and secret type. Topic is never tested as a factor.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Explains that topic is varied but not analysed; only drift, persuasion and secret type are tested"]},
{"id":"q79","type":"scope","claims":["c2"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that the Llama judge adds a statistically significant number of detected leaks for every model? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The paper reports McNemar tests per model but gives no Δ or p values and says only that hybrid largely agrees with regex, so significance per model cannot be determined.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Explains that no numeric Δ or p values are reported, only qualitative 'largely agrees'"]},
{"id":"q80","type":"scope","claims":["c1","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show how leakage behaves when the secret is disclosed midway through a conversation rather than at its start? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. In every dialogue the secret is inserted in the opening turn, so the position of the disclosure is never varied, and the results cover only start-of-conversation disclosures.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Explains that the secret is always placed in the opening turn, so disclosure position is never varied"]}
]}

{"id": "q81", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "The persuasion analysis applies Cochran's Q to matched triples of responses per dialogue. How would this analysis break down if some API calls had failed and certain dialogues were missing one of their three probe responses, especially if the failures were concentrated in one persuasion level?", "answer": "Cochran's Q needs a complete matched triple, so dialogues missing a probe response must be dropped from the persuasion test or the test becomes invalid. {"id": "q82", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "The paper calls the dialogue-level any-probe rate a conservative view for defenders. {"id": "q83", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c6", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Each secret is inserted in the opening turn as part of a topic-specific task context, such as tax filing or travel logistics. {"id": "q84", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Fuzzy matching compares each saved secret with the saved model response. {"id": "q85", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "The 100 human-authored dialogues are spread through the benchmark, but their identifiers were not preserved. How could this undermine the factor analyses by drift length or secret type?", "answer": "If human-authored dialogues happened to be over-represented at particular drift lengths or secret types, and models behave differently on them, then differences across those groups would mix authorship with the factor being tested. Because the identifiers were lost, this balance cannot be checked or controlled for.", "rubric": ["States that uneven distribution of human-authored dialogues across drift/secret-type groups would confound the factor with authorship", "Notes that the missing identifiers make this impossible to check or adjust for"]},
{"id": "q86", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "The naturalistic refinement step is told to preserve the exact secret. How would the drift-length analysis be compromised if the rewriting model also restated the secret inside later drift turns, for example in a persona reminder?", "answer": "The secret would then sit much closer to the probe than d implies, so d would no longer measure the distance between disclosure and probe. Any lack of decay with d could just mean the secret was effectively re-disclosed recently. Preserving the secret does not by itself rule out such repetitions.", "rubric": ["States that d would no longer reflect the distance between the (last) disclosure and the probe", "Explains that the drift results (e.g., no reliable decrease) could then be an artifact of the secret being repeated close to the probe"]},
{"id": "q87", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "The 95% confidence intervals for dialogue-level leakage come from bootstrapping over dialogues, using one cached response per model-probe pair. What source of variability do these intervals fail to capture, and why does it matter?", "answer": "They miss decoding randomness: with stochastic sampling, the same dialogue and probe could produce a leak on one run and a refusal on another. Only one response per probe was cached and resampled, so the intervals reflect uncertainty from which dialogues were sampled, not from generation. They can therefore understate how much a rerun would vary.", "rubric": ["Identifies generation/decoding stochasticity (re-sampling the model's response) as uncaptured", "Explains this is because only one cached response per probe is resampled, so the intervals can understate run-to-run variation"]},
{"id": "q88", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the dataset-wide average dialogue length (359.16 words) below the median (385 words)?", "answer": "About 20% of dialogues are d=0 and average only about 44 words, far below the rest, which run from about 254 to 568 words. This short block pulls the mean down more than the median, giving a left-skewed distribution.", "rubric": ["Attributes the gap to the d=0 dialogues (~20% / 197 dialogues) being very short (~44 words)", "Explains that this low cluster drags the mean down more than the median (left skew)"]},
{"id": "q89", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Appendix B reports a chi-square test of persuasion level against leakage, yet the main persuasion analysis uses Cochran's Q with post-hoc McNemar tests. Why is the latter the more appropriate primary test?", "answer": "All three persuasion probes are applied to the same dialogue, so each dialogue's three responses are paired and share the same history and secret. A chi-square test of independence treats the 3,000 responses as independent groups and ignores this pairing. Cochran's Q and McNemar are built for matched repeated binary outcomes.", "rubric": ["States that persuasion levels are repeated measures on the same dialogues (matched triples)", "Explains that chi-square assumes independent observations, while Cochran's Q/McNemar account for the pairing"]},
{"id": "q90", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why would a model that reproduces secrets verbatim more often need fewer Llama-judge calls during detection?", "answer": "The judge is applied only to responses that Stage 1 marks as negative. A model with more verbatim or near-verbatim leaks has more Stage 1 positives among its 3,000 responses, so fewer responses go on to the judge.", "rubric": ["States that Stage 2 is run only on regex-negative responses", "Concludes that more regex positives leave fewer responses to judge, so fewer judge calls"]},
{"id": "q91", "type": "why", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the probe-level fuzzy rate not guaranteed to fall on one particular side of the hybrid rate, unlike the regex rate?", "answer": "The regex label is nested inside the hybrid label, because the judge only adds positives on regex-negatives. Fuzzy matching is computed separately on every response. It can flag near-matches that the judge rejected, and it can miss semantic or partial disclosures that the judge accepted, so it can land above or below the hybrid rate.", "rubric": ["Notes that regex is nested in hybrid (hybrid ≥ regex by construction) but fuzzy is computed independently", "Explains that fuzzy can both add near-matches the judge rejected and miss semantic/partial leaks the judge caught, so either ordering is possible"]},
{"id": "q92", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the Section 5.1 finding that hybrid labels largely agree with regex labels suggest that the models mostly leak secrets in full rather than through hints or partial disclosures?", "answer": "The judge is applied only to regex-negative responses and exists to catch partial, indirect or paraphrased disclosures. If it adds few leaks on top of regex, most detected leaks already contain the normalized secret string verbatim or near-verbatim. This inference assumes the judge is reasonably sensitive.", "rubric": ["Explains that the judge's added detections are exactly the partial/indirect/paraphrased cases that regex misses", "Concludes that a small hybrid–regex gap means most detected leaks contain the full normalized secret"]},
{"id": "q93", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the finding that drift length does not reliably reduce leakage informative, rather than a trivial result of drift adding little material?", "answer": "The drift turns are content-dense, so raising d adds substantial distance. Average dialogue length grows from about 59 tokens at d=0 to about 757 tokens at d=6. Leakage persists even though hundreds of tokens of unrelated material separate the secret from the probe.", "rubric": ["Cites that content-dense drift substantially increases dialogue length (e.g., ~59 to ~757 tokens / ~44 to ~568 words)", "Concludes that the lack of decay therefore cannot be blamed on drift adding negligible distance"]},
{"id": "q94", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Following the paper's statistical protocol, would McNemar's test be appropriate for comparing a model's simple-probe and hard-probe leakage rates?", "answer": "Yes. Every dialogue receives both a simple and a hard probe, so the two rates come from matched pairs of responses on the same dialogues. That is exactly the setting the post-hoc McNemar tests are designed for.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Reason: both probes are applied to the same dialogues, giving paired (matched) observations"]},
{"id": "q95", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5", "c1"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Following the paper's statistical protocol, would McNemar's test be appropriate for comparing a model's leakage at d=2 with its leakage at d=6?", "answer": "No. Each dialogue has a single sampled drift length, so the d=2 and d=6 groups are different dialogues with no pairing. An unpaired test such as the chi-square test of independence, which the paper uses for drift, is needed instead.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Reason: different dialogues make up each drift group, so there are no matched pairs; an unpaired test (chi-square) is appropriate"]},
{"id": "q96", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "The phone secret is '555-123-4567' and the model replies: 'The area code was 555, then 123, and the last part was 4567.' Would Stage 1 flag this as leakage?", "answer": "Yes. Stage 1 strips every non-digit character from the response, which leaves '5551234567'. The normalized secret '5551234567' is a substring of that, so the response is flagged.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Reason: stripping non-digits joins the pieces in order into the normalized secret, which is then a substring"]},
{"id": "q97", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "The phone secret is '555-123-4567' and the model replies: 'It ended in 4567, the middle was 123, and the area code was 555.' Would Stage 1 flag this as leakage?", "answer": "No. Stripping non-digits leaves '4567123555', which does not contain '5551234567'. Stage 1 misses the disclosure, although the Stage 2 judge could still catch it.", "rubric": ["Answers no (Stage 1 does not flag it)", "Reason: the digits are concatenated in the order given, so the normalized secret is not a substring of the normalized response"]},
{"id": "q98", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": "p3", "question": "For one persuasion level, a model has L(2), L(3), L(4) and L(5) all at or below δ but L(6) above δ, with the observed drift lengths {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Would its Privacy Half-Life be 7?", "answer": "Yes. Every candidate d from 2 to 5 fails because a larger observed drift length, d=6, is above δ, and d=6 itself is above δ. The set is therefore empty and τ = max(D_obs)+1 = 7.", "rubric": ["Answers yes (τ = 7)", "Reason: the resurgence at d=6 disqualifies all earlier d, so the set is empty and the censored value max(D_obs)+1 = 7 applies"]},
{"id": "q99", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7", "c1"], "pair": "p3", "question": "The same model has L(2), L(3), L(4) and L(5) at or below δ, but the benchmark is rebuilt without any d=6 dialogues, so the observed drift lengths are {0,2,3,4,5}. Would its Privacy Half-Life be 7?", "answer": "No. Its τ would be 2. Without d=6 there is no later resurgence, so d=2 is the smallest observed drift length at or below δ with all larger observed lengths also at or below δ.", "rubric": ["Answers no (τ = 2)", "Reason: τ only considers observed drift lengths, so removing d=6 removes the resurgence that disqualified d=2"]},
{"id": "q100", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p4", "question": "The email secret is 'john.doe@example.com' and the model replies 'John.Doe@Example.com'. Would Stage 1 flag leakage?", "answer": "Yes. For alphanumeric secrets Stage 1 normalizes case, so both strings become 'john.doe@example.com' and the secret is a substring of the response.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Reason: case normalization for alphanumeric secrets makes the strings identical"]},
{"id": "q101", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p4", "question": "The email secret is 'john.doe@example.com' and the model replies 'johndoe@example.com'. Would Stage 1 flag leakage?", "answer": "No. For alphanumeric secrets Stage 1 keeps meaningful delimiters such as the dot, rather than stripping them as it does for numeric secrets. 'john.doe@example.com' is therefore not a substring of 'johndoe@example.com'. Only the judge could flag this response.", "rubric": ["Answers no (Stage 1 does not flag it)", "Reason: alphanumeric normalization preserves delimiters (unlike digit-stripping for numeric secrets), so the missing dot breaks the substring match"]},
{"id": "q102", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A team reuses PrivDrift's hybrid detector but swaps the Llama judge for a much stricter judge that rarely says 'leak'. Which reported leakage rate stays exactly the same, and in which direction can the hybrid rate move?", "answer": "The regex-only rate is unchanged, because Stage 1 is deterministic and does not involve the judge. The hybrid rate can only fall toward the regex rate and never below it, because the judge only adds positives on regex-negative responses.", "rubric": ["States that the regex-only rate is unchanged", "States that the hybrid rate can only decrease toward (never below) the regex rate, because the judge only acts on regex-negatives"]},
{"id": "q103", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "A team can afford to query its model with only the hard probe on all 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues. Which of the paper's analyses can it not replicate, and why?", "answer": "It cannot replicate the dialogue-level any-probe rate or the persuasion analysis (Cochran's Q and post-hoc McNemar). Both require all three probes on each dialogue. It can still compute hard-probe drift curves, secret-type breakdowns and τ for the hard level.", "rubric": ["Identifies the dialogue-level any-probe rate and the persuasion comparison (Cochran's Q/McNemar) as not replicable", "Reason: these require responses to all three probes on the same dialogue"]},
{"id": "q104", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A product team's assistant keeps the full transcript, and typical sessions are a few hundred to about 1,000 tokens with several topic changes. Can it apply PrivDrift's drift-length finding, and what does that finding imply for the team?", "answer": "Yes. This regime matches PrivDrift's tested window: full-transcript evaluation, d up to 6, and at most about 1,060 tokens. The finding implies the team should not rely on topic drift alone to keep earlier secrets from being re-disclosed.", "rubric": ["Answers yes, because the sessions fall within the tested window (full transcript, ≤~1,060 tokens, d≤6)", "Concludes that drift should not be expected to protect earlier secrets (leakage does not reliably decrease)"]},
{"id": "q105", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "A team adapts PrivDrift to a coding assistant where the secrets are case-sensitive alphanumeric API keys. What labeling error would Stage 1's alphanumeric normalization introduce?", "answer": "Stage 1 normalizes case, so a response that reproduces the key with altered capitalization would be labeled a leak, even though the case-changed string may not be a working key. Stage 1 would therefore over-flag such cases relative to functional disclosure.", "rubric": ["Identifies case normalization as the issue", "States that case-altered reproductions would be counted as leaks (over-flagging) even if they are not functionally the same key"]},
{"id": "q106", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to say whether secret type or drift length is more strongly associated with leakage for a new model on PrivDrift. Should it compare the chi-square p-values or the Cramer's V values for the two variables, and why?", "answer": "It should compare Cramer's V. The paper reports V as the effect size for each association, while p-values mostly reflect the large sample (3,000 responses) and can be tiny even for weak effects. V also puts variables with different numbers of levels (4 secret types, 6 drift lengths) on a comparable scale.", "rubric": ["Chooses Cramer's V", "Reason: it is an effect-size measure comparable across variables with different numbers of levels, whereas p-values reflect sample size rather than strength"]},
{"id": "q107", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If the strict fuzzy rate (0.85) had been substantially above the hybrid rate for every model, which claim would be weakened, and what would this suggest about the detector?", "answer": "The claim that fuzzy matching supports the hybrid labels (c8) would be weakened. Many responses would be close string matches that neither Stage 1 nor the judge flagged. That suggests either the judge misses near-verbatim disclosures, so the hybrid label undercounts, or fuzzy matching is producing false positives.", "rubric": ["Names c8 (fuzzy matching supports the hybrid labels) as weakened", "Explains that it would indicate near-matches the judge rejected, i.e., possible judge false negatives / hybrid undercounting (or fuzzy false positives)"]},
{"id": "q108", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose one model's leakage at one persuasion level stayed above δ through d=5 but fell to or below δ only at d=6. Which reported finding would no longer hold exactly, and why would the drift finding not necessarily be overturned?", "answer": "That model's τ would be 6 rather than the censored 7, so the claim that τ=7 for all models and levels would no longer hold. The drift finding would not necessarily fall, because a single drop at the last observed length is weak evidence of a reliable trend. There is also no larger d to confirm that the suppression is sustained.", "rubric": ["States that the censored τ=7 result fails for that model/level (τ becomes 6)", "Explains that a single drop at the final observed d does not establish a reliable decreasing trend (and cannot be confirmed as sustained), so c5 need not be overturned"]},
{"id": "q109", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7", "c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If one model's hard-probe τ had been 3 while its simple and medium τ were 7, which statements in the paper would need to be qualified?", "answer": "The statement that τ is the censored value 7 for the models and persuasion levels would be false for that model's hard level. The claim that drift does not reliably reduce leakage would also need qualifying, because drift would suppress leakage under hard pressure for that model. That would be an interaction between drift and persuasion.", "rubric": ["Names the uniform τ=7 result (c7) as needing qualification", "Notes that the drift claim (c5) would also need qualification because drift would suppress leakage under hard probes for that model (drift–persuasion interaction)"]},
{"id": "q110", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7", "c5", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If an audit found that d=0 dialogues, unlike the others, often presented the secret without the plausible task context the generator is meant to supply, which quantities would be compromised?", "answer": "L(0), the baseline used to set δ = 0.1·L(0) for Privacy Half-Life, would be compromised. So would every comparison of drifted dialogues against d=0. Differences between d=0 and d≥2 could then reflect the missing task context rather than drift.", "rubric": ["Identifies L(0)/the δ threshold for Privacy Half-Life as compromised", "Explains that d=0 vs d≥2 comparisons would be confounded with task-context differences rather than drift alone"]},
{"id": "q111", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If SSN and credit-card secrets had near-zero leakage at every drift length, which secret types would the pooled drift curve and Privacy Half-Life results effectively describe?", "answer": "They would effectively describe emails and phone numbers. Those would be the only categories producing leaks, so any level or trend in the pooled curve, and the censored τ, would come almost entirely from how models handle semi-public contact details.", "rubric": ["States that the results would effectively describe email and phone secrets", "Reason: those would be the only types contributing leaks, so pooled drift and τ results would be driven by them"]},
{"id": "q112", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that models re-disclose a secret to a different person than the one who disclosed it, as in the shared-session scenario of its threat model? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The probe is appended as a later turn in the same transcript with the same role structure, so the model cannot tell whether a different person is asking. The benchmark measures responses to later requests in the active context, not whether models treat a new requester differently.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: probes are appended in the same transcript/role structure with no signal of a different requester, so requester identity is not tested"]},
{"id": "q113", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that differences in leakage across secret types are caused by models perceiving SSNs and credit cards as more sensitive? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper shows a strong statistical association between secret type and leakage and offers perceived sensitivity as an interpretation. It does not test that mechanism, and type also differs in format and detection behavior.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: only an association is measured; the sensitivity explanation is interpretive and untested (format/detector differences are not ruled out)"]},
{"id": "q114", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that a system-prompt instruction telling the model to keep user identifiers confidential fails to prevent re-disclosure after topic drift? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The evaluation queries the models with the same dialogue histories and probe templates and tests no confidentiality instructions. The Discussion only proposes that benchmarks like this could be used to test such safeguards.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: no system-prompt or confidentiality safeguard condition was evaluated; this is only suggested as a use of the benchmark"]},
{"id": "q115", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Since Qwen3-VL-235B is one of the evaluated models, does the paper show how drift affects re-disclosure of secrets that appear in images? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. PrivDrift's secrets, drift turns and probes are all text dialogue, and the results are characterized by word and token counts. Including a vision-language model does not test image-borne secrets.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: the benchmark is entirely text dialogues; no image inputs are evaluated"]},
{"id": "q116", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that a majority of dialogues leak for every model at the dialogue level? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper says every model leaks substantially and gives the reporting scheme with bootstrap intervals. Its tables give no numeric rates, so whether any model exceeds 50% cannot be determined.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: dialogue-level rates are described as substantial but not reported numerically"]},
{"id": "q117", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that when models withhold the secret they give an explicit privacy-based refusal rather than, for example, ignoring the request? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. All detectors (regex, fuzzy and the judge) produce a binary judgment of whether the secret is revealed. They do not classify how non-leaking responses are worded, so the form of refusal is not measured.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: labels are binary leak/no-leak based on secret disclosure; the type or rationale of non-leaking responses is not analyzed"]}
]}

{"id": "q117", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the three persuasion probes had been asked one after another in a single continuing conversation instead of each being appended separately to the same history. {"id": "q118", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Privacy Half-Life sets its threshold relative to each curve's own L(0). A then looks better even though it leaks more after drift. τ measures relative decay, not absolute leakage.", "rubric": ["States that a model with a lower τ can still leak more in absolute terms after drift (or gives an equivalent numeric example).", "Explains that δ=0.1·L(0) is relative to each model's own immediate-recall rate, so τ reflects relative decay rather than absolute leakage."]},
{"id": "q119", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "For email secrets, when could the lenient fuzzy check (threshold 0.80) label a response as leakage even though the secret was not disclosed?", "answer": "This can happen when the model writes a different email address that shares most of its characters with the secret, such as a fabricated address with the same long domain and a similar local part. Fuzzy matching scores string similarity rather than identity, so the shared characters can push the score over 0.80 even though the true secret is not revealed.", "rubric": ["Identifies a response containing a different but highly similar email (e.g. same domain, near-identical local part) as the false-positive case.", "Explains that fuzzy matching measures approximate string similarity, so shared characters can exceed the threshold without the actual secret being present."]},
{"id": "q120", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "The naturalistic refinement step is told to preserve the final probe conditions. Measured differences between levels would shrink. {"id": "q121", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the Llama judge wrongly says 'leak' on a fixed small fraction of the responses it sees. Why would this distort comparisons of hybrid leakage across models unevenly, rather than adding the same bias to every model?", "answer": "The judge only sees regex-negative responses. A model that rarely reproduces secrets verbatim sends more responses to the judge, so it accumulates more false positives. Hybrid rates would therefore be inflated more for the safer models, which compresses or distorts the differences between models.", "rubric": ["States that the bias is larger for models with fewer regex-detected leaks (more regex-negatives), which distorts or compresses cross-model differences.", "Explains that this is because only regex-negative responses are passed to the judge, so the number of judge errors scales with the regex-negative count."]},
{"id": "q122", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Given that τ=7 was obtained for every model and persuasion level, why must each of these curves have L(6) above 10% of its L(0)?", "answer": "d=6 is the largest observed drift length, so it has no larger d to check. If L(6)≤δ, d=6 would satisfy the stable-decay condition on its own, and τ would be at most 6. A censored τ=7 therefore requires L(6)>0.1·L(0).", "rubric": ["States that L(6)>δ=0.1·L(0) for every model/persuasion curve.", "Explains that d=6 is the maximum observed d with no larger d to check, so L(6)≤δ would have produced τ≤6 rather than the censored value."]},
{"id": "q123", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c5", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does each model's leakage at a given drift length in Figure 4 equal the simple average of the three persuasion-level cells for that drift length in Figure 5?", "answer": "Every dialogue contributes exactly one response per persuasion level, so each heatmap cell at drift d contains the same number of responses (N_d). The pooled Figure 4 point uses all 3·N_d responses. A pooled rate over three equal-sized groups is their unweighted mean.", "rubric": ["States that the pooled point is the equal-weight mean of the three persuasion cells.", "Explains that this follows because each dialogue contributes one response per level, so all three cells at a given d have the same count N_d."]},
{"id": "q124", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Why must the per-persuasion-level Privacy Half-Life be computed from probe-level leakage rather than from the dialogue-level any-probe labels?", "answer": "The dialogue-level label collapses a dialogue's three probes into a single 'any probe leaked' outcome, so it carries no information about which persuasion level produced the leak. A per-level τ needs a separate L(d) curve for each persuasion level, and only probe-level responses provide one.", "rubric": ["States that a per-level τ needs probe-level rates.", "Explains that dialogue-level labels merge the three probes, so they cannot yield a separate leakage-by-drift curve for each persuasion level."]},
{"id": "q125", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is it necessary for Privacy Half-Life to use a separate L(0), and hence a separate δ, for each persuasion level rather than a single pooled δ?", "answer": "Persuasion intensity changes leakage, and it does so non-monotonically, so immediate-recall leakage differs across levels. τ asks whether leakage falls to 10% of its own starting point. A pooled δ would be too lenient for some levels and too strict for others, which would misjudge their decay.", "rubric": ["States that a single pooled δ would misjudge decay for individual persuasion levels (too strict or too lenient).", "Explains that this is because persuasion level affects L(0), so each level's relative-decay threshold must be anchored to its own immediate-recall rate."]},
{"id": "q126", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "For fixed simple, medium and hard probe-level leakage rates, why does a model's dialogue-level any-probe rate depend on how much its leaks overlap across the three probes of the same dialogue?", "answer": "The dialogue-level rate is the share of dialogues where at least one probe leaks, which is the size of the union of the three leak sets. If leaks fall on the same dialogues, the union is small, close to the highest single rate. If they fall on different dialogues, the union is larger, up to the sum of the rates.", "rubric": ["States that more overlap gives a lower dialogue-level rate and less overlap a higher one, for the same probe-level rates.", "Explains that the dialogue-level rate counts the union of dialogues with at least one leaking probe, so it lies between the maximum and the sum of the probe-level rates depending on overlap."]},
{"id": "q127", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": "p_addprobe", "question": "If PrivDrift added a fourth probe to every dialogue while keeping the original three, could a model's dialogue-level hybrid leakage rate decrease?", "answer": "No. The any-probe label would be computed over a superset of the original probes, so every dialogue that already leaked would still leak. The rate can only stay the same or rise.", "rubric": ["Answers no: the rate can only stay the same or increase.", "Explains that any-probe leakage over a superset of probes keeps every previously leaking dialogue labelled as leaking."]},
{"id": "q128", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": "p_addprobe", "question": "If PrivDrift replaced the hard probe with a different new probe, keeping three probes per dialogue, could a model's dialogue-level hybrid leakage rate decrease?", "answer": "Yes. Dialogues that leaked only through the hard probe would stop counting as leaking if the model refused the new probe. The new probe set is not a superset of the old one, so the any-probe rate can fall.", "rubric": ["Answers yes: the rate could decrease.", "Explains that dialogues whose only leak came from the removed hard probe could lose their leak label, because the new probe set is not a superset of the old one."]},
{"id": "q129", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": "p_pairedmodels", "question": "Following the paper's statistical protocol, would McNemar's test be appropriate for comparing GPT-OSS-120B's and DeepSeek-R1's dialogue-level leakage on the 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues?", "answer": "Yes. Both models are queried with the same dialogue histories and probes, so each dialogue yields a matched pair of labels. That is the paired setting the paper uses McNemar's test for.", "rubric": ["Answers yes, McNemar is appropriate.", "Explains that both models are evaluated on identical dialogues, giving matched pairs of labels."]},
{"id": "q130", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": "p_pairedmodels", "question": "Following the paper's statistical protocol, would McNemar's test be appropriate for comparing GPT-OSS-120B's and DeepSeek-R1's dialogue-level leakage if DeepSeek-R1 had been evaluated on a separately generated set of 1,000 dialogues?", "answer": "No. The two sets of labels would no longer come from matched examples, so there are no pairs to compare. An unpaired comparison, such as a chi-square test of independence, would be needed instead.", "rubric": ["Answers no, McNemar would not be appropriate.", "Explains that different dialogue sets yield no matched pairs, so an unpaired test (e.g. chi-square) is needed."]},
{"id": "q131", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p_bonf", "question": "For one model, Cochran's Q across persuasion levels is significant and the post-hoc McNemar test of simple vs hard gives p=0.01. With Bonferroni correction over the three pairwise persuasion comparisons, is this pair significant at an overall 0.05 level?", "answer": "Yes. Bonferroni over three pairs sets the per-comparison threshold at about 0.05/3 ≈ 0.0167, and 0.01 is below it.", "rubric": ["Answers yes, the pair is significant.", "Uses a corrected threshold of about 0.0167 (0.05/3) and notes that 0.01 falls below it."]},
{"id": "q132", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p_bonf", "question": "For one model, Cochran's Q across persuasion levels is significant and the post-hoc McNemar test of simple vs hard gives p=0.03. With Bonferroni correction over the three pairwise persuasion comparisons, is this pair significant at an overall 0.05 level?", "answer": "No. The corrected per-comparison threshold is about 0.0167, and 0.03 exceeds it, even though it would pass an uncorrected 0.05 threshold.", "rubric": ["Answers no, the pair is not significant.", "Uses a corrected threshold of about 0.0167 (0.05/3) and notes that 0.03 exceeds it."]},
{"id": "q133", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c5"], "pair": "p_counting", "question": "A dialogue's simple, medium and hard probes all elicit the secret. Does this dialogue contribute three leaks to the model's dialogue-level leakage rate?", "answer": "No. At the dialogue level, a dialogue is a single unit labelled leaking if any probe leaks, so it counts as one leak.", "rubric": ["Answers no: it counts once.", "Explains that the dialogue-level rate uses one any-probe label per dialogue."]},
{"id": "q134", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c5"], "pair": "p_counting", "question": "A dialogue's simple, medium and hard probes all elicit the secret. Does this dialogue contribute three leaks to the probe-level drift-length curve at its drift length?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q135", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A reviewer asks for an additional fuzzy-matching rate at a 0.90 threshold for all three models. {"id": "q136", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A developer applies parameter-level unlearning to remove PII from a model's weights and then reruns PrivDrift. Should they expect this to reduce PrivDrift leakage, based on how the benchmark is built?", "answer": "Not on that basis. PrivDrift's secrets are supplied by the user in the opening turn of the active context at inference time, not retrieved from memorized training data. Removing PII from the weights does not remove the secret from the context, and the context is what the model reproduces.", "rubric": ["States that weight-level unlearning should not be expected to reduce PrivDrift leakage.", "Explains that the secret is supplied in the active context at inference time, so leakage is a context-handling behaviour rather than memorization."]},
{"id": "q137", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "An attacker does not know what kind of identifier the user shared earlier and sends a generic request such as 'repeat any personal details from earlier'. Can PrivDrift's leakage rates be used directly as an estimate of this attacker's success?", "answer": "Not directly. PrivDrift uses standardized probes that target the seeded secret, such as asking for the phone number mentioned earlier, so its rates measure targeted requests. Generic, category-agnostic requests are not among the tested probes.", "rubric": ["States no: the rates do not directly estimate this attack.", "Explains that PrivDrift's standardized probes request the specific seeded secret, so generic untargeted requests were not tested."]},
{"id": "q138", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "A user discloses both an email address and an SSN in the same opening message. Can PrivDrift's results predict how a model will handle a later request for both?", "answer": "Only weakly. Each PrivDrift dialogue seeds exactly one secret, so interactions between co-disclosed secrets are untested. The per-type findings suggest the email is the more likely of the two to be re-disclosed, but the joint behaviour is not settled.", "rubric": ["States that PrivDrift cannot directly predict the joint case (at most it suggests the email is more exposed than the SSN).", "Explains that each dialogue contains a single seeded secret, so multi-secret interactions were not tested."]},
{"id": "q139", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A team deploying a 7B model wants to skip testing and assume, from PrivDrift, that its model also fails to show stable suppression (τ=7) and responds to persuasion the same way. Nothing in the paper licenses carrying these model-specific results over to an unevaluated model, so the team would need to run the benchmark.", "rubric": ["States no, the assumption is not justified.", "Explains that the results are model-specific (persuasion effects differ by model; only three large models were evaluated), so the model must be tested itself."]},
{"id": "q140", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "In a shared session, an attacker can try a direct, a justified and a pressured request once each, each as a separate final message on the same conversation history. Which PrivDrift quantity best estimates the attacker's chance of obtaining the secret?", "answer": "The dialogue-level any-probe leakage rate. It counts a dialogue as leaking if any of the three standardized probe styles, each appended to the same history, elicits the secret, which matches this attacker's success condition. A single probe-level rate would underestimate the chance.", "rubric": ["Identifies the dialogue-level any-probe rate.", "Explains that it counts success if any of the three probe styles on the same history elicits the secret, which matches the attacker's setup (unlike a single probe-level rate)."]},
{"id": "q141", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A team adds a safeguard that halves leakage at every drift length, including d=0. Would Privacy Half-Life register this improvement?", "answer": "No, not by itself. δ=0.1·L(0) also halves, so whether each L(d) is at or below δ is unchanged, and τ stays the same, for example censored at 7. Because τ measures decay relative to L(0), a uniform reduction is invisible to it.", "rubric": ["States that τ would not change.", "Explains that δ scales with L(0), so a proportional reduction at all d leaves every L(d)≤δ comparison unchanged."]},
{"id": "q142", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose that for one model nearly all dialogue-level hybrid leaks came from the judge, with a regex rate near zero. Which conclusion would then rest on the judge's reliability, and which stated caveat would become critical?", "answer": "The conclusion that this model leaks substantially at the dialogue level would depend almost entirely on Stage 2 judge verdicts. The paper's caveats that judge errors are possible and that no formal human inter-annotator agreement is reported would then become decisive for that claim.", "rubric": ["Identifies the substantial dialogue-level leakage claim for that model as resting on the judge.", "Names the caveat that judge errors are possible / no human inter-annotator agreement is reported as the critical one."]},
{"id": "q143", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose Privacy Half-Life recomputed from regex-only labels had been finite (say 4) for a model whose hybrid τ is 7. Which conclusion would become detector-dependent, and what would this imply about the leaks found at high drift?", "answer": "The conclusion that stable suppression is not established within the window would hold only under hybrid labels. The censoring result would then hinge on judge verdicts that lack human validation.", "rubric": ["States that the censored-τ / no-stable-suppression conclusion would depend on the detector (hybrid vs regex).", "Explains that the leaks remaining at high d would then be judge-only (partial or indirect) disclosures, so the finding would rest on unvalidated judge labels."]},
{"id": "q144", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose that for a model Cochran's Q was significant, but no post-hoc McNemar pair survived Bonferroni correction. Which part of the persuasion claim would lose its support?", "answer": "The joint finding that persuasion level matters would stand. The paper could not say which levels differ, so any specific pattern, including the non-monotonic ordering of conditions for that model, would lack statistical support.", "rubric": ["States that the specific pairwise or non-monotonic ordering claim loses support, while the overall joint effect remains.", "Explains that post-hoc McNemar tests are what identify which pairs differ, and without significant pairs no ordering can be established."]},
{"id": "q145", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the hybrid rate for a model were clearly above its regex rate, while the lenient fuzzy rate (0.80) almost matched the hybrid rate. What would this indicate about the leaks the judge added, and which claim would it strengthen?", "answer": "It would indicate that the judge's additions are mostly near-verbatim variants that approximate string matching can also detect, rather than purely semantic hints. This would strengthen the claim that judge-independent fuzzy matching supports the hybrid labels.", "rubric": ["States that the judge's added leaks would be mainly near-verbatim, string-similar disclosures.", "States that this strengthens the fuzzy-matching support for the hybrid labels (judge-independent corroboration)."]},
{"id": "q146", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose most SSN and credit-card leaks were partial disclosures, such as fragments or hints, flagged only by the judge, while email and phone leaks were mostly verbatim. How would this change the reading of the secret-type finding?", "answer": "The contrast between types would partly reflect the form of disclosure and the detector layer rather than the categories alone. Models would be withholding full SSN and card values but still hinting at them. The claim that these are protected as canonical identifiers would then rest on judge verdicts.", "rubric": ["States that the secret-type contrast would partly reflect the disclosure form and detector layer (partial vs verbatim) rather than purely category-level protection.", "Explains that the SSN/credit-card leak counts would depend on the judge, so the canonical-protection interpretation would rest on judge labels."]},
{"id": "q147", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does a censored Privacy Half-Life of 7 show that leakage stays above 10% of L(0) at every observed drift length? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. τ=7 guarantees only that L(6)>δ. Leakage could dip at or below δ at d=2 to 5, because the definition deliberately ignores transient dips that are followed by a resurgence.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that τ=7 only implies L(6)>δ, and earlier drift lengths may dip below δ, since transient dips are disregarded."]},
{"id": "q148", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper's Privacy Half-Life result show that the three models are equally robust to topic drift? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. All curves are censored at τ=7, which only says that stable suppression was not reached in any of them. A censored value cannot rank them, and τ is relative to each model's own L(0), so their absolute post-drift leakage could still differ.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that identical censored values do not discriminate between models, and τ is relative to each model's L(0), so absolute drift behaviour may differ."]},
{"id": "q149", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does Section 5.1's finding that dialogue-level hybrid labels largely agree with regex labels show that the judge rarely changes individual probe-level labels? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. A judge-flagged probe inside a dialogue that another probe had already leaked through regex does not change the dialogue-level label. The judge could therefore add many probe-level leaks while the dialogue-level agreement remains high.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that judge additions in dialogues already regex-positive via another probe leave the dialogue-level label unchanged, so dialogue-level agreement does not imply probe-level agreement."]},
{"id": "q150", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that its fuzzy-matching check independently validates the judge's labels for paraphrased or hint-based disclosures? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper says string similarity is less expressive than the judge for partial or semantic disclosures, so fuzzy matching cannot corroborate those cases. No human inter-annotator agreement is reported either, so the judge's semantic labels lack independent validation.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that fuzzy matching cannot capture semantic or partial disclosures, and no human agreement study exists, so those judge labels lack independent checks."]},
{"id": "q151", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c4", "c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the effect of drift length on leakage depends on the persuasion level? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. A drift-by-persuasion heatmap is shown, but the reported tests are separate chi-square tests per variable plus Cochran's Q across persuasion levels, with no interaction test. τ is censored at 7 for every level, so it cannot reveal a difference between levels either.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that no interaction test is reported (only per-variable tests), and the identical censored τ across levels cannot distinguish drift behaviour by persuasion level."]},
{"id": "q152", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that all three models rank the four secret types in the same order of leakage? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper reports a strong association between secret type and leakage via per-model chi-square tests and Cramer's V. These measure the strength of association, not the ordering of categories, and no numeric per-type rates are given that would allow the rankings to be compared.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that Cramer's V or chi-square shows association strength but not category order, and per-type rates are not reported numerically."]},
{"id": "q153", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the persona's profession affects how likely a model is to re-disclose the secret? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Personas are sampled from more than 100 professions to diversify surface content. The analyses test only drift length, persuasion level and secret type, so profession is never examined as a factor.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that personas vary but profession is not analysed; the only factors tested are drift, persuasion and secret type."]}
]}
