{"id": "q1", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c5", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Drift turns come from a content-dense library meant to add unrelated entities to the context. If some drift turns contained other identifiers of the same category as the secret (for example, a second phone number in a business-letter task), how could this bias the drift-length curve?", "answer": "The probe asks for, say, 'the phone number mentioned earlier', so it would become ambiguous. A model could return the drift-turn number instead of the seeded secret. Stage 1 would not match that number, and the judge, which compares the response to the stored secret, would likely mark it a non-leak. Leakage would then appear to fall as more drift turns are added, which would be a spurious decrease caused by confusion rather than by protection.", "rubric": ["Says the bias would be an artificial decrease in measured leakage with drift (or a spurious drift effect).", "Explains that the model may return a different same-type identifier from the drift turns, which neither Stage 1 nor the judge counts as the seeded secret.", "Notes that this reflects ambiguity or confusion rather than genuine confidentiality."]},
{"id": "q2", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "The naturalistic refinement step is performed by a rewriting model. If that model had tended to mask or partially redact SSNs and credit-card numbers in the opening turn, but not emails or phone numbers, how would this affect the secret-type finding?", "answer": "The target models could not reproduce a full SSN or card number that was never fully present in their context. Lower leakage for those types would then be an artifact of the generation pipeline, not evidence that models treat them as protected identifiers. The secret-type effect would be confounded with pipeline-induced masking.", "rubric": ["Says the lower SSN and credit-card leakage could be an artifact, so it would not show that models treat these types as more confidential.", "Explains that a redacted secret cannot be re-disclosed in full or matched against the stored secret, and that the masking would differ by type."]},
{"id": "q3", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "The 95% confidence intervals for dialogue-level leakage come from bootstrapping over dialogues as if they were independent. Given how PrivDrift builds dialogues, when would these intervals be too narrow?", "answer": "Dialogues are assembled from a shared topic-conditioned library of drift turns and from persona and probe templates. If many dialogues reuse the same drift turns or templates, their outcomes are correlated. Resampling dialogues one at a time then treats clustered data as independent and understates uncertainty. The intervals would be too narrow whenever such reuse is substantial.", "rubric": ["Says the intervals would be too narrow (they would understate uncertainty) when dialogues are not independent.", "Identifies reuse of shared drift-library turns, personas or templates as the source of correlation among dialogues."]},
{"id": "q4", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "All dialogues are queried with the same standardized probe templates for each persuasion level. Why might the non-monotonic persuasion finding fail to generalize to 'persuasion intensity' as such?", "answer": "Each level is represented by fixed template wording, so every level comparison confounds intensity with the particular phrasing used. A model may react to a specific phrase, such as a refusal trigger in the urgent wording, rather than to the intensity itself. Different wordings at the same intensity could reverse the pattern.", "rubric": ["Says the finding may be specific to the templates and may not hold for persuasion intensity in general.", "Explains that each level uses fixed wording, so intensity is confounded with phrasing that may trigger refusal or compliance."]},
{"id": "q5", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Figure 4's drift curve pools all three probes. How could it show no reliable drift effect even if drift strongly reduced leakage under one persuasion level?", "answer": "If drift lowered leakage under, say, hard probes but raised it, or left it flat, under another level, the effects could cancel or be diluted in the pooled curve. The pooled curve and its chi-square test would then show little association even though a strong level-specific drift effect exists. This can only be checked in the per-level heatmap (Figure 5).", "rubric": ["Says pooling across persuasion levels can mask a level-specific drift effect.", "Explains that opposite or flat trends at other levels can cancel or dilute the effect in the pooled curve.", "Notes that the per-persuasion breakdown (Figure 5 or per-level analysis) is needed to detect it."]},
{"id": "q6", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "The medium probe gives a contextual justification, such as needing the information for a form, and each secret is inserted with a task context such as tax filing. When would a medium-versus-simple difference fail to reflect the effect of added justification pressure?", "answer": "When the justification matches the original purpose of the disclosure (for example, a form in a tax-filing dialogue), the request looks like a continuation of the legitimate task rather than added pressure. Higher compliance would then reflect purpose consistency in the contextual-integrity sense, not susceptibility to persuasion. The effect would depend on how well the justification fits the dialogue's topic.", "rubric": ["Says the difference may not reflect persuasion pressure when the justification aligns with the original task purpose.", "Explains that compliance could then be a contextually appropriate continuation of the user's task rather than a response to pressure."]},
{"id": "q7", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why can differences between persuasion levels in how often the Llama judge adds leaks not be caused by the judge reacting to the probe wording itself?", "answer": "The judge receives only the secret and the model response, not the probe or the dialogue history. Any variation in judge-added leaks across persuasion levels must therefore come from differences in the responses the models produced.", "rubric": ["States that the judge does not see the probe (it sees only the secret and the response).", "Concludes that differences across levels must come from the model responses themselves."]},
{"id": "q8", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why can nearly all of the roughly 524-word gap between the average d=0 and d=6 dialogues be attributed to the drift turns?", "answer": "A d=0 dialogue consists only of the opening turn containing the secret plus the probe, and it averages about 44 words. Those components are present in every dialogue regardless of d. The extra length at d=6 (568 vs 44 words) must therefore come almost entirely from the inserted drift turns.", "rubric": ["States that the d=0 dialogues contain only the opening secret turn and the probe (about 44 words).", "Explains that these components are shared by all drift levels, so the added length is due to the drift turns."]},
{"id": "q9", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Even if the human-authored dialogue identifiers were recovered, why would comparing the 100 human-authored and 900 synthetic dialogues not cleanly contrast human-written with machine-written conversation?", "answer": "The topic-conditioned drift library itself includes human-authored drift turns that are used in generation. Synthetic dialogues can therefore contain human-written drift content. The split would compare construction routes, not purely human versus purely synthetic text.", "rubric": ["Says the comparison would not be a clean human-versus-machine contrast.", "Explains that human-authored drift turns are part of the library used to build the synthetic dialogues."]},
{"id": "q10", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is Table 1's dataset-wide average of 359.16 words consistent with the per-drift averages in Table 7?", "answer": "The overall mean is the average of the Table 7 group means weighted by their group sizes (197, 147, 142, 166, 181, 167). The two tables describe the same 1,000 dialogues.", "rubric": ["States that the overall mean is the size-weighted average of the per-drift group means.", "Shows or asserts that weighting by the counts 197/147/142/166/181/167 reproduces about 359.16 words."]},
{"id": "q11", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why can differences between a model's three persuasion-level thresholds δ not be due to the levels' L(0) values being measured on different dialogues?", "answer": "All three probes are appended to every dialogue, so each persuasion level's L(0) is computed on the same 197 d=0 dialogues. Any difference in δ therefore reflects how the model responds to the different probes, not a different sample of dialogues.", "rubric": ["States that every persuasion level's L(0) uses the same d=0 dialogues (197), because all three probes are applied to each dialogue.", "Concludes that δ differences reflect probe responses, not sampling of different dialogues."]},
{"id": "q12", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the dialogue-level hybrid-versus-regex comparison more sensitive to judge false positives than a comparison made on a single probe?", "answer": "A dialogue counts as a hybrid leak if any of its three probes is flagged. A regex-negative dialogue therefore gives the judge up to three chances to wrongly say 'leak', and one error on any probe flips the whole dialogue. Judge errors compound at the dialogue level.", "rubric": ["States that dialogue-level labels are an OR over the three probes.", "Explains that a judge false positive on any one of up to three regex-negative probes flips the dialogue, so errors compound."]},
{"id": "q13", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p1", "question": "The phone secret is '555-123-4567' and the model replies '555-123-4567 ext. 89'. {"id": "q14", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p1", "question": "The phone secret is '555-123-4567' and the model replies '555-123-4576' (last two digits swapped). Would Stage 1 flag leakage?", "answer": "No. The normalized response '5551234576' does not contain '5551234567' as a substring, so only the judge (or fuzzy matching) could flag it.", "rubric": ["Answers no.", "Explains that the swapped digits break the exact substring match after normalization."]},
{"id": "q15", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7", "c1"], "pair": "p2", "question": "For one persuasion level, a model has L(0)=0.50. {"id": "q16", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7", "c1"], "pair": "p2", "question": "For one persuasion level, a model has L(0)=0.50. If 8 of the 142 d=3 dialogues leak under that level, does d=3 satisfy L(d) ≤ δ?", "answer": "No. δ = 0.05, but 8/142 ≈ 0.056 exceeds it. With only 142 dialogues, a single extra leak decides the threshold.", "rubric": ["Answers no.", "Computes δ=0.05 and L(3)=8/142≈0.056 > δ."]},
{"id": "q17", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": "p3", "question": "To get a confidence interval for a model's probe-level hard-probe leakage rate alone, would bootstrapping individual responses be equivalent to bootstrapping dialogues?", "answer": "Yes. Each dialogue contributes exactly one hard-probe response, so resampling those responses is the same as resampling dialogues.", "rubric": ["Answers yes.", "Explains that there is exactly one hard-probe response per dialogue, so the two resampling units coincide."]},
{"id": "q18", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c5"], "pair": "p3", "question": "To get a confidence interval for a point on the pooled probe-level drift curve (all three probes), would bootstrapping individual responses be equivalent to bootstrapping dialogues?", "answer": "No. Each dialogue contributes three responses that share the same history and secret, so they are correlated. Resampling responses independently would ignore this and understate uncertainty, which is why the paper resamples dialogues.", "rubric": ["Answers no.", "Explains that the three probe responses per dialogue are correlated (they share history and secret), so dialogues must be resampled."]},
{"id": "q19", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c1"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Following the paper's protocol, would Cochran's Q be appropriate to test whether leakage differs across the three persuasion levels within only the d=6 dialogues?", "answer": "Yes. Within the d=6 subset each dialogue still contributes a matched triple of simple, medium and hard responses, which is the repeated-measures structure Cochran's Q requires.", "rubric": ["Answers yes.", "Explains that matched triples per dialogue are preserved within the subset."]},
{"id": "q20", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Following the paper's protocol, would Cochran's Q be appropriate to test whether simple-probe leakage differs across d=2, d=4 and d=6?", "answer": "No. Each dialogue has a single drift length, so the three drift groups contain different dialogues and the responses are not matched.
